title: Hedging in Academic Writing
text:
Hedging refers to the use of cautious language that signals a writer's uncertainty or reluctance to make absolute claims. In academic writing, verbs such as 'suggest' and 'appear' and modal expressions such as 'may' and 'could' are common examples. Writers rely on these devices because scientific findings are rarely conclusive. Without them, a claim may be treated as more certain than the evidence allows.

Hedges also serve a social function, since they protect writers from criticism and invite readers to evaluate the argument. By contrast, boosters such as 'clearly' or 'undoubtedly' express strong confidence and can sound assertive. Consequently, experienced researchers balance the two carefully. Overuse of boosters may weaken credibility, whereas excessive hedging can make a text seem vague.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, which expressions are common examples of hedging in academic writing?
options: Verbs such as 'suggest' and 'appear' and modals such as 'may' and 'could'
Numbers and percentages taken from experiments

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what do boosters express?
options: A request for readers to evaluate the argument

questions.text: What can be inferred about why researchers avoid absolute claims?
options: Journal editors always reject absolute claims
Scientific findings are rarely conclusive, so absolute claims may overstate the evidence
Hedging is used only by inexperienced writers
Readers prefer texts that contain no evidence at all

questions.text: What does the passage imply about a text that contains excessive hedging?
options: It may appear vague and lack confidence
It is always more credible than a balanced text
It contains too many strong claims
It is written mainly for readers who disagree with the writer

vocabulary.definition: words that express strong confidence in a claim
the quality of being trusted and believed
not clear or precise in meaning

paragraph_translations: La atenuación (hedging) se refiere al uso de un lenguaje cauteloso que indica la incertidumbre del autor o su reticencia a hacer afirmaciones absolutas. En la escritura académica, verbos como 'suggest' y 'appear' y expresiones modales como 'may' y 'could' son ejemplos comunes. Los autores recurren a estos recursos porque los hallazgos científicos rara vez son concluyentes. Sin ellos, una afirmación podría considerarse más segura de lo que permite la evidencia.

Las atenuaciones también cumplen una función social, ya que protegen a los autores de las críticas e invitan a los lectores a evaluar el argumento. En cambio, los potenciadores como 'clearly' o 'undoubtedly' expresan una gran confianza y pueden sonar categóricos. Por ello, los investigadores experimentados equilibran cuidadosamente ambos recursos. El uso excesivo de potenciadores puede debilitar la credibilidad, mientras que una atenuación excesiva puede hacer que el texto parezca vago.
